22 The warning signal on an ambulance has a frequency of 600 Hz. The speed of sound is 330 m s–1.
The ambulance is travelling with a constant velocity of 25 m s–1 towards an observer. The
ambulance passes, and then moves away from the observer with no change in velocity.
initial position
of ambulance
final position
of ambulance
observer
Which overall change in observed frequency takes place between the times at which the
ambulance is a long way behind the observer and when it is a long way in front of the observer?
A
49 Hz
B
84 Hz
C
91 Hz
D
98 Hz

hints: Notice the phrase a long way in front and a long way behind means the ambulance motion is directly towards then directly away from the observer.
Recall the Doppler observed wavelength is shortened on approach by $v_s T$ and lengthened on recession by $v_s T$, so use $f' = f v/(v - v_s)$ and $f'' = f v/(v + v_s)$.
Calculate both observed frequencies with $600 \text{ Hz}$, $330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $25 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, then subtract the lower receding frequency from the higher approaching frequency.
walkthrough: Identify the given data: source frequency $f_o = 600 \text{ Hz}$, speed of sound $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, source speed $v_s = 25 \text{ m s}^{-1}$, with stationary observer.
State the Doppler rule for a moving source: approaching compresses waves so $f_{approach} = f_o v/(v - v_s)$, while receding stretches waves so $f_{recede} = f_o v/(v + v_s)$.
Find the overall change from approaching to receding: $\Delta f = 649.2 - 557.7 \approx 91.5 \text{ Hz}$, a decrease of about $91 \text{ Hz}$.

A.explanation: This is only the increase from $600 \text{ Hz}$ to the approaching frequency, about $649 \text{ Hz} - 600 \text{ Hz}$, not the full approaching to receding change.

B.explanation: This value is too small and does not match $f_o v/(v-v_s) - f_o v/(v+v_s)$ with $f_o = 600 \text{ Hz}$, $v = 330 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ and $v_s = 25 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

C.explanation: The approaching frequency is about $649 \text{ Hz}$ and the receding frequency is about $558 \text{ Hz}$, giving a drop of about $91 \text{ Hz}$.

D.explanation: This is about twice the approaching shift alone, $2 \times (649 - 600) \text{ Hz}$, and ignores that the receding shift is smaller than the approaching shift.
